A reading group summarizes Kasch's foundational claim as: 'projection and undercraft are just two independent skills, so a performer's projection score tells you nothing at all about their undercraft.' What is the most important thing this summary gets wrong?

A. Projection and undercraft scores are simply uncorrelated, so a strong projector is exactly as likely to have strong undercraft as weak, with no direction to the relationship either way.
B. Projection and undercraft are really one underlying stage-skill quality, so a performer who commands an audience's attention is also likely to be strong at holding a scene together backstage.
C. Projection and undercraft are not merely unrelated but negatively associated, so a strong projection score does predict something specific: on average, weaker undercraft skill, not an absence of any pattern.
D. Training projection and training undercraft are independent processes, so a performer who spent years training projection has not thereby lost any capacity for undercraft skill.

Troupe A's anchor performer needed exactly one backstage correction all night and made it invisibly; Troupe B's anchor performer needed thirty corrections and caught every single one invisibly. Both score a Fen index of 1.0. What does this pair of nights show about the Fen index and the correction load?

A. Troupe A's performer must be the less skilled of the two, since catching thirty corrections cleanly all night is a harder demonstration of skill than catching just one.
B. Since both performers scored an identical 1.0, their nights were equally smooth, with roughly the same number of things going wrong backstage for each of them.
C. The Fen index is a rate, not a count -- it says nothing about how often correction was needed, so the matching score hides that Troupe B's performer carried a far heavier correction load.
D. The Fen index also counts corrections that could conceivably have arisen but never did, which is why Troupe B's larger set of possible problems still produced the same score.

A touring director is casting a new show. Performer X reliably draws the loudest audience reactions but has struggled in rehearsal to catch missed cues without being noticed. Performer Y draws little audience attention but has caught nearly every backstage problem cleanly and invisibly. Based on Kasch's casting findings, how should the director assign the lead and anchor positions?

A. X should be cast as the lead, and because leads carry the most responsibility for holding a scene together, X's struggles with missed cues are the most urgent problem to fix.
B. X should be cast as the lead, the highest-projection-demand position, and Y as the anchor, the highest-correction-load, lowest-visibility position.
C. Y should be cast as the anchor, and because anchors absorb the correction load entirely, X as lead will need to do no backstage correction work at all.
D. X should be cast as the anchor, since anchor is the show's most prominent and structurally important position, and X is clearly the stronger overall performer of the two.

A touring manager boasts: 'Our Fen index has been a flawless 1.0 for six months straight -- our undercraft has never been better.' Using Kasch's account of rescue, repair, and correction load, which objection has the most support?

A. A flawless Fen index built only from rescues, alongside a flat or growing correction load, is the diagnostic picture Kasch treats as most dangerous -- the troupe may have merely gotten skilled at surviving recurring problems, not repairing them.
B. The stronger objection is that a lower Fen index paired with a shrinking correction load would actually be the worse diagnostic picture, since the raw success rate has visibly declined over time.
C. There is no real objection to raise here: a flawless Fen index sustained for six months is, on its own, clear proof that backstage craft has genuinely gotten better, regardless of what the correction load happens to be doing.
D. The best objection is that the manager is likely counting a run of especially effective rescues as repairs, since a repair is really just a rescue performed with enough confidence to look permanent.

Over a touring season, a troupe's audience-rated gloss score climbs steadily month after month. What can we responsibly conclude about the troupe's undercraft from this trend alone, per Kasch's account of the gloss effect?

A. Very little on its own -- gloss tracks projection reliably, but it can rise even as the Fen index falls, since a confident cover of a visible stumble often reads as tighter craft than it is.
B. Gloss should track the Fen index just as reliably as it tracks projection quality, so a rising gloss score is solid evidence that the troupe's undercraft has kept pace as well.
C. Gloss and the Fen index are really two measurements of the same underlying quality of a show, so a rise in one is good evidence of a matching rise in the other across an entire touring season.
D. The undercraft has clearly improved, since an audience rating a show as more seamless is responding to a real increase in how well backstage problems are caught, night after night, throughout the season.

A veteran performer known for commanding entire houses with high-energy work turns out, in backstage logs, to have one of the lowest Fen indices in her troupe. A colleague concludes she must simply care less about the ensemble than her castmates do. Which explanation does Kasch's account of the halo fallacy actually support?

A. She simply cares less about the ensemble than her castmates do, and her weak backstage record is exactly the evidence a director needs to see that this is true, regardless of what audiences think of her.
B. Her low Fen index and her strong projection are simply unrelated facts about her as a performer, and their both showing up in the same person is nothing more than coincidence, unconnected to how either skill is trained.
C. Since she commands the audience's attention more completely than anyone else in the troupe, she is clearly the strongest overall performer and should also be the one most reliable backstage when something goes wrong.
D. Sustaining projection at full scale narrows a performer's peripheral awareness of the rest of the stage, which leaves less attention free for backstage correction -- an attentional limit, not a difference in effort, care, or commitment to the ensemble.

Kasch found that average Fen index peaks for troupes of five to seven performers -- the core band -- and declines for troupes below four and troupes above ten. A director notices that both a three-person troupe and a fourteen-person troupe show unusually low Fen indices, and concludes both are suffering the identical problem: not enough attentive people to catch backstage issues. What is wrong with this explanation?

A. The two declines are mechanically different: the small troupe lacks redundancy to cover someone pulled into projection, while the large troupe has too many signaling pairs to stay coordinated even though enough people are available.
B. Both troupes likely have low audience-rated gloss scores, and since gloss and the Fen index move together, their low ratings from audiences explain why their measured Fen indices are also low.
C. Larger troupes should always show a higher Fen index than smaller ones, since more performers means more hands free to cover a problem, so the fourteen-person troupe's low score is most likely a measurement error.
D. Nothing is wrong with it -- both troupes are simply short on attentive people, whether that shortage comes from having too few performers or from the demands of a fourteen-person show spreading everyone thin.

A student summarizes the field's history this way: 'Ferrant showed that the projection/undercraft distinction itself doesn't hold up.' Which classification of Ferrant's actual objection is accurate?

A. Ferrant accepted the projection/undercraft distinction and objected only to how 'invisible' was measured -- she argued backstage observers were folding two different audience responses, true non-detection and noticed-but-forgiven, into a single category.
B. Ferrant showed that Kasch's original backstage-observer method already separated a truly unnoticed correction from one the audience noticed but forgave, and her real contribution was mainly statistical refinement.
C. Ferrant's real objection was that projection, not undercraft, is what audiences are responding to when they rate a show's seamlessness, which is the same conflation the gloss effect describes.
D. Ferrant rejected the distinction wholesale, arguing that undercraft is really just an unrecognized form of projection, and that backstage observers have simply been sorting one real skill into two invented categories.
